cf.title: Set 1s WaitLatch timeout if standby limit has expired in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin

input.subject: Set 1s WaitLatch timeout if standby limit has expired in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived the panel at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The problem is stated with a concrete race, two independent field reports support it (messages #4 and #6), and the fix is a bounded timeout confined to standby.c. The open items are a test, the backpatch branch list, the unmeasured broadcast cost and the order relative to the parallel loop rewrite; they belong to committability and later review levels.

brief.title: Bounded startup wait on expired buffer pin conflicts on standby
brief.problem: After max_standby_streaming_delay expires, the startup process sends the buffer pin conflict signal once and then waits with no timeout. A backend that pins the buffer after that signal is never told to cancel, so replay can stall indefinitely. Dmytro saw it on 18.4 and Andrey on a 17.11 production standby, with lag reaching 5h41m.
brief.proposed_design: When the standby limit has already expired, the startup process waits on its latch with a 1s timeout instead of waiting until UnpinBuffer() wakes it. On timeout it rechecks the pin count and sends the conflict signal again, so late pinners get canceled. v3 calls WaitLatch directly in standby.c and leaves proc.c and proc.h unchanged.
user_visible_surface: Behavior change: after the standby limit expires, backends holding a conflicting pin are canceled about one second after they take it, instead of possibly never.
author_claims: A backend can pin the buffer after the startup process sent the conflict signal and never receive another one, so replay stalls.
A 1s timeout on the expired path lets the startup process resend the signal and cancel new conflicting backends.
v3 does not touch proc.c or proc.h, so backpatching should be easy (Shihao).
Reproduced on 18.4 and 17.11; v3 cancels the late pinner in about one second (Dmytro, Andrey, João).
With max_standby_streaming_delay = -1 the wait stays unbounded, and the non-expired path is unchanged (João).
brief.thread_state: Shihao, Andrey and João tested v3 and support it, and João asked for a test, commit trailers and a backpatch line. Xuneng accepts the diagnosis but worries about repeated broadcasts and would prefer an event-driven fix, with no concrete design yet.
unclear: The patch has no regression or TAP test; nobody has said whether a timing-dependent test is acceptable.
No branch list for backpatching is stated, and v3 needs signal and wait-event names adapted on 17.
The interaction with the patch from [1], which rewrites the same wait as a loop, is not settled.
CF entries 6444 and 6445 both point to this thread; the record does not say which one stays open.
No one has measured the cost of a broadcast every second on standbys with many backends.

prior_attempts.title: Revert "Get rid of the dedicated latch for signaling the startup process".
prior_attempts.quote: Because it broke the assumption that the startup process waiting for the recovery conflict on buffer pin should be waken up only by buffer unpin or the timeout enabled in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin().
prior_attempts.reason:
Revert ac22929a26, as well as the followup fix 113d3591b8. Because it broke
the assumption that the startup process waiting for the recovery conflict
on buffer pin should be waken up only by buffer unpin or the timeout enabled
in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin(). It caused, for example,
SIGHUP signal handler or walreceiver process to wake that startup process
up unnecessarily frequently.

Additionally, add the comments about why that dedicated latch that
the reverted patch tried to get rid of should not be removed.

Thanks to Kyotaro Horiguchi for the discussion.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 removed the dedicated wakeup latch, so unrelated events woke the startup process. v3 keeps that latch and adds only a timeout inside ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin(), which is one of the two wakeup sources the revert message allows.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The patch changes how the startup process waits during a buffer pin recovery conflict on a hot standby.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: v1 and v2 touch proc.c and proc.h; v3 is reported to leave both unchanged.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The patch narrows an existing way for any standby session to stall replay with a late buffer pin.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The CF entry targets stable branches, and v3 needs signal and wait-event names adapted on 17.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a timed wait in recovery conflict code that few people know, and a parallel patch rewrites the same wait.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The startup process resends the conflict signal to backends every second while replay is blocked after the limit expires.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which stable branches should receive the fix, and what does the adapted patch look like on 17, where the signal and wait-event names differ?
What does one conflict broadcast per second cost on a standby with many backends while replay stays blocked?
Should this fix go in before or after the parallel patch that rewrites the same wait as a loop, and which one gets rebased?
Can a test reproduce the late pin deterministically, for example with an injection point, without depending on timing?
Which of the CommitFest entries 6444 and 6445 stays open for this thread?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the startup process, recovery conflict handling and the buffer pin wakeup path. Álvaro Herrera created the CF entry in message #2 but has not reviewed the patch in the visible thread.
committability.liability: A behavior change in recovery conflict handling on every supported branch that gets the backpatch, with no regression test so far. The owner also signs for the resend cost on busy standbys and for the merge with the parallel loop rewrite.
committability.author_follow_up: The author rebased and posted v2 in message #3 after seven months of silence on the thread, and a v3 followed. Shihao Zhong moved the entry to the next CommitFest and stays as reviewer.

priority.reason: The fix is small and confined to standby.c, and two field reports show replay stalls of up to 5h41m on hot standbys. Three reviewers tested v3, but no committer who knows the area has reviewed it, and the entry has been open across two CommitFests.

provisional_note: The code was not read, and v3 is known only from the brief. The recheck of the pin count after a timeout, the latch reset order and the interaction with the deadlock-check timeout could not be judged.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use latch instead of pg_usleep for standby recovery conflicts
precedents_retrieved.summary: Simon Riggs added a CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS() call to the standby's wait for recovery conflict resolution, and Michael Paquier then proposed a deeper fix for HEAD. That fix replaces the pg_usleep() in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithVirtualXIDs(), which can sleep up to 1s, with WaitLatch() and a new wait event.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Review found that CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS() does nothing in the startup process and that WL_LATCH_SET has no effect because MyLatch is never set there. Michael Paquier then judged that calling HandleStartupProcInterrupts() would reload the GUC context in the middle of replaying a record. He concluded that all conflict code paths should use a latch, and returned the patch with feedback as time ran short.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Calling
HandleStartupProcInterrupts() is actually dangerous I think, because
it would reload the GUC context while replaying a record.

precedents_retrieved.title: Start WAL streaming as early as possible, without waiting for startup process to finish replaying existing WAL. This helps synchronous replication to resume quickly when significant replay lag has been built up.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch starts the WAL receiver on a standby before the startup process finishes replaying WAL already in pg_wal, so synchronous commits on the primary are not held up by replay lag. A GUC, wal_receiver_start_condition, picks when the receiver starts, and the start LSN is the beginning of the most recently flushed segment, found by reading the first page of each segment in pg_wal.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected that the start LSN is roughly the consistency point, so streaming begins too early when many local segments, often copied by hand, are still left to replay. He also rejected the WAL page checks as hard to maintain, noted that the patch requests streaming when PrimaryConnInfo is not set, and suggested a WAL reader scan from the redo point to find the real end of local WAL. The entry stayed "Waiting on Author" after this review and was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Your patch would cause streaming to begin too early, and a manual copy of segments is not a rare thing as in some environments a bulk copy of segments can make the catchup of a standby faster than streaming.

precedents_retrieved.title: Don't ignore recovery conflict interrupt on blocked writing
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes a backend that is blocked writing results to the client socket handle recovery conflict interrupts instead of ignoring them, and terminates the session because protocol sync cannot be kept. It targets standbys where a dead or slow client keeps a buffer pin and blocks WAL replay until the TCP retransmission timeout, about 15 minutes.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund showed that the patch did not promote the ERROR to FATAL and only ended the session through InteractiveBackend()'s EOF handling on stdin. He also showed that error reporting runs with interrupts held, so a conflict during a blocked write of an error message is never handled. The author posted a reworked approach that returns a write error instead, but no reply follows it. The visible messages do not show why the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Unfortunately I suspect that this means any protection we'd get from this version of the patch is rather incomplete - if the recovery conflict is triggered while not blocked, we'll ERROR out and report the message with interrupts held.

precedents_retrieved.title: Synchronous replay mode for avoiding stale reads on hot standbys
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a synchronous_replay mode in which a commit on the primary waits until all available hot standbys have replayed it, and standbys hold time-limited leases that the primary revokes when they lag more than synchronous_replay_max_lag. A synchronous_replay read transaction on a standby without a valid lease raises a new error 40P02, so clients get a read-follows-write guarantee without tracking LSN tokens.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last shown message is a rebase in February 2019, and the withdrawal in July 2019 is not explained. Open items at that point included missing TAP tests, an unexplained replication protocol corruption bug, Masahiko Sawada's questions about how the new setting relates to synchronous_commit, and the author's own note that Simon Riggs had not been convinced of the approach.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add more TAP coverage for archive status with crash recovery of standbys
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Add more TAP coverage for archive status with crash recovery of standbys
Reverted commit(s): Remove some unstable parts from new TAP test for archive status check
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This part of the test was included originally in 4e87c48, but got
reverted as of f9c1b8d because of timing issues in the test, where,
after more analysis, we found that the standbys may not have recovered
from the archives all the segments needed by the test.  This stabilizes
the test by making sure that standbys replay up to the position returned
by pg_switch_wal(), meaning that all segments are recovered before the
manual checkpoint that tests WAL segment recycling and its interactions
with archive status files.

precedents_retrieved.title: Simplify standby state machine a bit in WaitForWALToBecomeAvailable()
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the standby state machine in WaitForWALToBecomeAvailable() set currentSource to XLOG_FROM_PG_WAL after a failed archive read, so XLogFileReadAnyTLI() no longer falls back to pg_wal itself. The current source is then passed to XLogFileReadAnyTLI() directly, without the XLOG_FROM_ANY special case.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier showed that the patch undoes commit 4d894b41. On HEAD, XLogFileReadAnyTLI() checks the archive and then pg_wal for each timeline in turn. With the patch it checks the archive for all timelines and only then pg_wal, so a segment with a higher TLI in pg_wal is no longer preferred. The author agreed and withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: And this patch basically undoes that, meaning that we would basically look at the archives first for all the expected TLIs, but only if no files were found in pg_wal/.

precedents_retrieved.title: Inconsistency in startup process's MyBackendId and procsignal array registration with ProcSignalInit()
precedents_retrieved.summary: In hot standby the startup process takes its procsignal slot as MaxBackends + MyAuxProcType + 1 but gets a different MyBackendId from SharedInvalBackendInit(), so SendProcSignal() using PGPROC->backendId misses it. The author proposed either making senders scan the procsignal array by PID with a comment on AuxiliaryPidGetProc(), or having the startup process pass a fixed BackendId to SharedInvalBackendInit() with one extra ProcState slot.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Kyotaro Horiguchi said the scan-and-comment options fix one inconsistency with another. With Andres Freund he moved the discussion to a larger redesign that replaces BackendId with pgprocno and removes the O(N) loops in sinvaladt.c, posted as a separate patch series. The author's last message asked whether that approach was acceptable, and no reply is shown before the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: 2 and 3 looks like fixing inconsistency by another inconsistency.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix cancelled queries when hot_standby_feedback = on
precedents_retrieved.summary: With hot_standby_feedback = on, standby queries still get cancelled when vacuum truncates a heap on the primary, because the AccessExclusiveLock taken for truncation is replayed on the standby. The final patch adds a new lock level, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE LOCAL, that vacuum uses for heap truncation and that is not WAL-logged, so standby queries must tolerate concurrent truncation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane showed that letting scans run during truncation leaves a race: concurrent scans can load to-be-truncated pages back into shared buffers before ftruncate, and reading past EOF on a standby can extend the relation. Alexander Korotkov agreed the patch had to be revised and sketched a new truncation design, but Robert Haas called it fragile and doubted it prevents stale buffers from being taken as valid. No new version followed, the existing patch failed initdb, and the entry was closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: If we ever have valid-looking buffers in shared_buffers after the corresponding data has been truncated away on disk, we've got to make sure that nobody ever confuses one of them with an actually-valid buffer.

precedents_retrieved.title: Replica sends an incorrect epoch in its hot standby feedback to the Master
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes a bug in Postgres 9.6, 10 and 11 where a replica's nextXid can move backward during WAL replay in RecordKnownAssignedTransactionIds, so hot standby feedback carries a wrong epoch and the master ignores the replica's xmin. The one-line fix advances nextXid only when the new value is higher, as similar code elsewhere does.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The withdrawal was not a rejection of the fix. The author registered the patch in the commitfest more than once, and David Steele marked the duplicate entries 2462 and 2463 as withdrawn. The visible messages show no objection, and Thomas Munro agreed the nextXid assignment looked wrong.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I have marked the duplicate entries 2462 and 2463 as withdrawn.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent proposed this fix, and no recorded reason applies against it. P1 is the closest: its rule allows a timeout set in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin(), which v3 adds. P2 and P4 cover different conflict paths, and P11 bears only on how stable a test would be. Message #5 cites a parallel patch that rewrites the same wait as a loop and keeps the expired path untimed, so the two patches do not apply together.

The patch adds no syntax, GUC, catalog object, dump content or psql change. After expiry, late conflicting queries get canceled, as max_standby_streaming_delay already documents, and Xuneng withdrew the 'promise' concern in message #11, so the backpatched behavior change matches the stated contract.

The proposal changes no persistent or cross-node state: no WAL record, on-disk format, catalog, protocol message or proc.h struct, so no pg_upgrade, mixed-version or extension ABI issue arises. [P1] was reverted for waking the startup process from unrelated sources, but this timeout is bounded and only applies after the standby limit has expired.

The proposal adds no new privilege, role, setting, view or message, so it creates no new security exposure. It shrinks an existing denial-of-service path: today any user who can connect to a hot standby can stall replay with a late buffer pin (message #4), and v3 cancels that session in about a second. The extra cost is one conflict broadcast per second, and it only runs while replay is already blocked. A user who keeps pinning again could already hold up replay before this patch, so this is not a new attack.

From the maintenance and fit angle, this is a small bugfix confined to standby.c, and v3 leaves proc.c and proc.h alone (message #5). It bounds a wait that already has a 1s deadlock-check wakeup before expiry, and that wait only happens on a standby already stalled by a conflict. The extra cost is one conflict signal per second per stalled buffer. Backends that hold no conflicting pin pay little for it. There is no new GUC, no API, no on-disk or WAL change, and core is the only place this can be fixed.

The extra wakeup comes from a timeout, which keeps the startup process woken only by unpin or a timeout. That fits the assumption [P1] protects. Xuneng's event-driven alternative has no design yet (message #12), and changing PinBuffer would add hot-path cost (message #10).

Open items do not support a rejection. No committer has engaged beyond Álvaro creating the CF entry. The order relative to the loop rewrite in [1] is not settled. There is no test, the backpatch branch list is not stated, and the broadcast cost on standbys with many backends is not measured. These belong under committability and level 4.

Postgres has no existing feature, setting or extension that resends the buffer pin conflict signal once the standby limit has expired. The workarounds in the thread, a manual pg_terminate_backend or a diagnostic signal to the startup process (messages #4, #6), need an operator to notice a stall that can last hours, so they do not meet the need. The fix sits inside the startup process wait in standby.c, where a hook or an extension cannot reach. The bounded wait reuses the existing WaitLatch and conflict-signal path and adds no second mechanism.

The demand is shown in the thread. It is a bugfix for a replay stall with independent field reports: Dmytro saw it several times on 18.4 (message #4), and Andrey saw it on a 17.11 production standby with 5h41m lag (message #6). The only workaround is a manual superuser wakeup of the startup process, and the cost of the fix falls only on standbys whose limit has already expired.
